pr_title: kubelet: Admission must exclude completed pods and avoid races
pr_body:
Fixes two issues with how the pod worker refactor calculated the
pods that admission could see (GetActivePods() and
filterOutTerminatedPods())

First, completed pods must be filtered from the "desired" state
for admission, which arguably should be happening earlier in
config. Exclude the two terminal pods states from GetActivePods()

Second, the previous check introduced with the pod worker lifecycle
ownership changes was subtly wrong for the admission use case.
Admission has to include pods that haven't yet hit the pod worker,
which CouldHaveRunningContainers was filtering out (because the
pod worker hasn't seen them). Introduce a weaker check -
IsPodKnownTerminated() - that returns true only if the pod is in
a known terminated state (no running containers AND known to pod
worker). This weaker check may only be called from components that
need admitted pods, not other kubelet subsystems.

This commit does not fix the long standing bug that force deleted
pods are omitted from admission checks, which must be fixed by
having GetActivePods() also include pods "still terminating".

issue_context.title: 1.22 regression: Kubelet rejects pods that use resources that should be freed by completed pods
issue_context.body:
#### What happened:

There appears to be a change of behavior / possible regression in k8s 1.22 with respect to pod lifecycle behavior.

We've started to see some cases when multiple pods are being created (often as part of a k8s job) the following will happen:

1. Multiple pods get created by e.g. job controller (e.g. say 5). Each pod in job requests majority of node memory so only one such pod can fit on node at a time.
2. Scheduler schedules [first] pod to node, rest (4 pods) stay in pending
3. Kubelet accepts first pod, runs it to completion
4. Next pod get scheduled to the node
5. Kubelet rejects the pod during pod admission, e.g. with `OutOfMemory`, despite the fact that the first pod has already completed successfully
6.  This results in many of pods backing the job getting into Failed phase and having to be recreated by job controller. The job can often get into BackofLimit exceeded to hitting backoffLimit.

The root issue seems to be a mismatch of when kubelet actually considers the pod to complete and what it reports to API server (which causes the followup pods to be scheduled to it). I'm still investigating further, but this may be related to the pod lifecycle changes in 1.22 -- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/102344

I've created a e2e test as minimal repro of this behavior -- https://github.com/bobbypage/kubernetes/blob/b8e2c5bec8f12d866493ecfccede3669377a7f0c/test/e2e/scheduling/job-completions.go

### 1.22.0 behavior

(Test fails)

```
# using checkout of https://github.com/bobbypage/kubernetes/tree/job-completions
$ make WHAT="test/e2e/e2e.test"
# kind config -- https://gist.github.com/69376696bbdba9c842f2bf07eb7cca15
$ kind create cluster --config ${HOME}/dev_scripts/kind-config-e2e.yaml --image kindest/node:v1.22.0
$ ./_output/bin/e2e.test -context kind-kind -ginkgo.focus="\[Feature:JobWithCompletions\]" --num-nodes=1 2>&1 | tee -i "/tmp/build-log.txt"
```

Shame we didn’t have an e2e which caught this given how easy the reproducer is.  This looks to be the opposite of the previous cpu admission bug (ignoring things that are terminating but not terminated).  We are weak on admission testing in general.

This potentially implies admission is looking at the wrong set of pods (> admitted + terminating).

Note there is already a bug in 1.21 and before where force deleted pods are incorrectly ignored from the set of allocated resources while they are terminating, but this doesn’t immediately seem to be that issue (since i doubt those jobs are being force deleted)

> this doesn’t immediately seem to be that issue (since i doubt those jobs are being force deleted)

yeah, there was no force deletion involved in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/104560#issuecomment-905205885 (or any deletion at all, actually... the completed pods just sat there, completed)

The set of admitted pods considered for pod count is everything in the pod manager filtered by filterOutTerminatingPods, which calls CouldHaveRunningContainers which returns true once a pod is seen by the workers (shortly after admission, and until we’ve confirmed via syncTerminatingPod that no containers are running).

Whatever the problem is it’s likely in the interaction of that.  A pod the pod worker hasn’t seen yet is also filtered out (that means bursts of pods can get in, which seems the opposite of this problem, and is the bug i mentioned before).

Edit: one wrong thing spotted while looking https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/104576 - I'm not sure it fixes the issue you're seeing, but it's definitely wrong for admission (admission is filtering the known pod set down to remove pods that are terminated, but shouldn't filter pods that aren't admitted yet).

This needs a node e2e reproducer that can run in serial (resource consumption is really hard to test from parallel, is slow in serial, and node e2e is back in a good state now) - @rphillips / @ehashman is that something either of you could help me with?  I believe the reason the existing tests don't catch this is the job controller is creating pods fast enough that we see races in admission (multiple pods are admitted in one call to HandlePodAdditions) that are not caught in the current serial node e2e admission tests which rarely create more than one at a time.

> I believe the reason the existing tests don't catch this is the job controller is creating pods fast enough that we see races in admission (multiple pods are admitted in one call to HandlePodAdditions) that are not caught in the current serial node e2e admission tests which rarely create more than one at a time.

Job pods still go through the scheduler to get assigned to a node, so even though the job controller can create pods in parallel, I'd still expect them to arrive at the node in an orderly fashion. It's still possible multiple arrive in a single HandlePodAdditions call, of course.

It seems like kubelet admission is using laggy information that doesn't reflect pod completion the kubelet itself wrote to the pod API.

The bug turned out to be much simpler.  Pods that are completed never go to the pod worker, so once a pod has reached terminal state it was being added back to the list of active pods.

The set of e2es that would have prevented this regression:

1. A node e2e that creates multiple pods at the same time and verifies that admission works correctly when HandlePodAdditions takes two pods at once
2. A node e2e that verifies that completed pods don't consume resources for admission purposes in the kubelet
3. A job controller e2e that attempts to verify some part of this reliably (ideally in a way that can be run in parallel e2e)

Linking here for completeness - a similar symptom might get exposed after this fix as described in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/106884.  The kubelet considers resources for terminating pods to be in use (they are!), but the scheduler ignores terminating pods and schedules new pods.  Because the kubelet now considers terminating pods, it rejects those rapidly rescheduled pods.  The follow up is more involved but requires the kubelet to allow pods to be potentially admitted that can't be run currently due to those terminating pods.  See the linked issue.
